ideas.title: Add a "Multi-Agent Systems" Concept entry
ideas.problem: The Concepts encyclopedia has no entry for multi-agent systems, yet the Deep-Dives section dedicates a full six-essay group to it and the Field Guide dedicates chapter x4. A reader on the Concepts index who wants to understand what multi-agent systems are has no on-ramp — they must jump directly into advanced essays or a full Field Guide chapter without foundational framing.
ideas.proposal: Add a new Concept entry with slug `multi-agent-systems`, group `Agentic AI`, positioned after `when-to-use-an-agent`. It should cover: why one agent is the default, what properties justify splitting (parallelism, specialization, context isolation), the coordination tax, and a clear pointer to the Deep-Dive group and Field Guide chapter x4. Requires bilingual HTML pair and a manifest.ts insertion.
ideas.evidence: src/content/concepts/manifest.ts (no multi-agent entry in Agentic AI group); src/content/deep-dives/groups/multi-agent-systems.ts (6-entry group); src/content/field-guide/manifest.ts (chapter x4 = multi-agent); src/content/field-guide/en/x4.html (extensive treatment with no foundational concept to point back to).
open_questions: Should it be placed before or after `when-to-use-an-agent` to preserve the logical progression from single-agent to multi-agent?
Should the group label remain `Agentic AI` or be a new `Agentic AI (Advanced)` sub-group?
ideas.mockup_hint: Four-step structure mirroring existing Agentic AI concepts. Step 1: the default position (one agent with tools). Step 2: the three honest justifications for splitting (parallelism, specialization, fault isolation). Step 3: the coordination tax — why multi-agent is not free. Step 4: a decision one-liner plus xref callout pointing to the Deep-Dives group and Field Guide chapter x4. One ASCII diagram showing a supervisor dispatching to two workers, similar to the trace blocks already used in x4.html. No code blocks needed. zh block identical in structure with all prose translated.

ideas.title: Expand Retrieval & RAG deep-dive group (currently only 2 entries)
ideas.problem: The Retrieval & RAG deep-dive group has exactly two entries (advanced-rag-architectures and graph-rag), making it the thinnest group on the site by a large margin. Every other mature group has 5–9 entries. Key topics are entirely absent: hybrid search / sparse-dense fusion, chunking strategy depth (semantic vs sliding-window vs late-chunking), query-rewriting and HyDE, and corpus management (freshness, deletion, poisoning aside from rag-security). The concept `what-is-rag` and `chunking-and-vector-search` have nowhere meaningful to graduate to within the group.
ideas.proposal: Add at minimum two essays to the Retrieval & RAG group: (1) `hybrid-search-and-reranking` covering BM25+dense fusion, reciprocal rank fusion, cross-encoder reranking, and the two-stage pipeline; (2) `query-transformation` covering HyDE, step-back prompting, query decomposition, and multi-query retrieval. A third candidate is `chunking-strategies` if content bandwidth allows. All three should be bilingual pairs added to `src/content/deep-dives/groups/retrieval-and-rag.ts`.
ideas.evidence: src/content/deep-dives/groups/retrieval-and-rag.ts (only 2 entries, order 40); other groups have 5-9 entries: architectures-and-patterns.ts (8), safety-and-security.ts (9), memory-and-context.ts (7); concepts `what-is-rag` and `chunking-and-vector-search` exist in src/content/concepts/manifest.ts with no graduate-to essays in this group.
open_questions: Should `rag-security` (currently in Safety & Security group) be cross-linked from this group or actually moved here — or is it better to leave it in Security given it's a security essay first?
Is `chunking-strategies` better as a third Retrieval & RAG deep-dive or as an expansion of the existing `chunking-and-vector-search` concept page?
ideas.mockup_hint: hybrid-search-and-reranking: open with 'Deep Dive · Retrieval & RAG' header. Two-part structure: Part 1 covers why dense retrieval fails for lexical queries and why sparse (BM25) fails for semantic ones, then explains reciprocal rank fusion as the cheap first-stage combination. Part 2 covers cross-encoder reranking as the second stage, with a code block showing a typical two-stage pipeline call. Close with a decision table: when one-stage suffices vs when to add reranking. query-transformation: similar structure — Step 1: why the user's raw query is often a bad retrieval signal; Step 2: HyDE (hypothetical document embeddings) with a one-function code block; Step 3: step-back prompting and query decomposition for multi-hop questions; Step 4: when to apply each and cost implications.

ideas.title: Add closing key-takeaway callout to long Deep-Dive entries
ideas.problem: No Deep-Dive essay on the site has a TL;DR, summary, or key-takeaways block. The Field Guide chapters have a `<div class='deliverable'>` section at the end (a checklist of concrete outputs), but Deep-Dives are essays that often run 400–800+ lines without any closing synthesis. A reader who skimmed to the bottom has no way to confirm what the durable mental models are. The `agentic-threat-model`, `llm-as-judge-for-agents`, and `advanced-rag-architectures` entries are all 400+ lines with no closing anchor.
ideas.proposal: Add a `<div class='callout tip'>` (or a new `.key-takeaways` callout if the design team creates one) at the end of each Deep-Dive essay that summarizes 3–5 durable takeaways in bullet form. This is an authoring convention change, not a schema change. Start with the 10 longest essays (by line count) and work down. The existing `.callout` class already handles bilingual content (both locales get the same structure). Coordinate with the design lens if a distinct `.c-takeaway` style is planned.
ideas.evidence: src/content/deep-dives/en/agentic-threat-model.html (no closing summary); src/content/deep-dives/en/llm-as-judge-for-agents.html (no closing summary); src/content/field-guide/en/e3.html (has a deliverable checklist at the end — Deep-Dives lack the equivalent); no TL;DR pattern found across any of the 75 deep-dive en/*.html files.
open_questions: Should the closing block use the existing `.callout tip` class or a new dedicated `.key-takeaways` class (which would need a CSS addition)?
Is 3–5 bullets the right scope, or would 1 durable sentence per heading section be cleaner?
ideas.mockup_hint:
At the very end of each Deep-Dive, after the last step div and before the closing , add:
Key takeaways
    with 3–5 short bullets that each capture one non-obvious, durable insight from the essay — not just a restatement of the section headings. Example for agentic-threat-model: 'Every text input channel (user, retrieval, tool output, memory) is an injection surface'; 'Attack surface composes — an agent using 3 tools inherits the weakest trust of all 3'; 'Least-privilege per tool, not per agent, is the correct granularity'. zh counterpart translates the bullet text faithfully.

ideas.title: Add a Concept entry bridging AI Foundations → Deep Learning depth
ideas.problem: The AI Foundations Concept group (8 entries) covers what-is-ai through temperature-and-sampling, but none of these 8 concepts has a corresponding graduate-to Deep-Dive essay. A reader who understands transformers at a high level and wants to go deeper has no on-site path — they must leave the wiki entirely. The gap is sharpest for two topics that are foundational for agentic AI practitioners: (1) how attention and positional encoding work in practice, and (2) what scaling laws mean for model selection decisions.
ideas.proposal: Add a new Deep-Dive essay `scaling-laws-and-capabilities` in a new group `AI Foundations & Models` (order 5, before Architectures & Patterns at order 10). The essay should cover: the Chinchilla compute-optimal frontier, the emergent capabilities debate, what scaling predicts vs. what it doesn't, and practical implications for builders (why you can't extrapolate benchmark rank to your task). A second candidate essay for the same group is `attention-and-position-encoding` for readers who want a practitioner's depth on why context windows behave as they do. This creates the first AI Foundations deep-dive path.
ideas.evidence: src/content/concepts/manifest.ts (all 8 AI Foundations entries map to zero deep-dives); src/content/deep-dives/groups/ (no group targeting AI Foundations — all 12 groups target agentic/building-block topics); src/content/concepts/en/what-is-an-llm.html and src/content/concepts/en/transformers-overview.html both reference scaling implicitly but have no graduate-to path.
open_questions: Should this be a new group (`AI Foundations & Models`) or should `scaling-laws-and-capabilities` be added to an existing group like Reasoning & Test-Time Compute?
Is the target reader a practitioner making model selection decisions, or someone who wants mechanistic understanding — these require different essays?
ideas.mockup_hint: scaling-laws-and-capabilities: Header 'Deep Dive · AI Foundations & Models'. Step 1: what a scaling law actually is — a power-law relationship between compute, data, parameters, and loss, with a simple log-log diagram rendered as ASCII. Step 2: the Chinchilla correction — why larger models were undertrained, and what compute-optimal training looks like. Step 3: emergent capabilities — what the term means, why the debate (smooth vs. sharp emergence) matters, and why benchmark contamination makes headlines unreliable. Step 4: builder implications — what scaling predicts (loss on training distribution) vs. what it does not predict (task performance, reasoning, agentic reliability). Close with a key-takeaway callout. zh counterpart: same structure, all prose translated, ASCII diagram byte-identical.

ideas.title: Thin intros on AI Ecosystem Concept pages (4 pages are under 62 lines)
ideas.problem: Four AI Ecosystem Concept pages — `inference-providers` (57 lines), `agent-frameworks` (58 lines), `modalities` (60 lines), and `reading-benchmarks` (60 lines) — are noticeably shallower than the site's other concepts (median ~88 lines). `agent-frameworks` has only 3 steps plus a closing paragraph, with the 'framework categories' step covering all major frameworks in 4 short paragraphs. `inference-providers` has just 3 steps. These pages read as stubs: they introduce the topic but stop before the practitioner decision layer (trade-offs, when to choose which option). By contrast, `cost-quality-latency` (71 lines) and `what-is-rag` (88 lines) in the same ecosystem reach the decision layer comfortably.
ideas.proposal: Expand each of the four shallow pages with a fourth step that delivers the practitioner decision layer: for `agent-frameworks`, a step on how to evaluate one without the hype (abstraction tax, escape hatches, observability — actually the content already has this in STEP 3, so the issue is STEP 2 breadth); for `inference-providers`, add a step comparing gateway vs. direct-API vs. self-host on the three axes of cost/latency/control; for `reading-benchmarks`, add a step on how to construct a 20-question private eval that beats any public leaderboard; for `modalities`, add a step on the architectural constraints of each modality combination (why vision-to-text and text-to-image are architecturally different from audio-in/audio-out).
ideas.evidence: Line counts from wc -l: inference-providers.html=57, agent-frameworks.html=58, modalities.html=60, reading-benchmarks.html=60; compared to median concept length of ~88 lines; src/content/concepts/en/agent-frameworks.html (3 substantive steps, no practitioner decision guidance beyond a warning callout).
open_questions: Should these be considered 'deliberately thin' as introductory concepts, or do they represent incomplete drafts?
For `agent-frameworks`, is the missing depth best added as a new STEP 4 or as expansion within STEP 2 (the categories section)?
ideas.mockup_hint: For inference-providers: add STEP 4 titled 'The three-axis trade-off: direct API vs gateway vs self-host'. Three columns (control, cost, latency) against three rows (first-party API, inference provider/gateway, self-hosted open weights). Use the `.threat-grid` table pattern already in the codebase. Close with a decision one-liner: 'Start with a first-party API; move to a gateway when you need multi-provider fallback or cost optimization; self-host only when data residency or latency at scale forces it.' zh: same table structure, all prose translated, table headers translated, no code blocks needed.

ideas.title: Missing Concept for 'Prompt Engineering Patterns' (few-shot has no graduate-to)
ideas.problem: The Concepts `prompting-basics`, `system-vs-user-prompts`, and `few-shot-prompting` together cover the fundamentals of prompting. But none of these three concepts has a corresponding graduate-to Deep-Dive essay covering advanced prompting techniques. A practitioner who understands few-shot prompting and wants to go deeper — to chain-of-thought variations, meta-prompting, role definition, structured system prompts for agents — has no on-site path. The only prompting-related Deep-Dive is `prompt-injection` (a security essay) and `prompt-finetune-or-rl` (a training decision essay). Advanced prompt design for agents is entirely absent.
ideas.proposal: Add a new Deep-Dive essay `advanced-prompt-engineering` to the Architectures & Patterns group (the most natural home, since prompt structure is an architectural decision for agents). The essay should cover: chain-of-thought variants (standard, zero-shot, least-to-most), structured system prompt anatomy for agentic tasks (persona, goal, tool context, constraints, output format), meta-prompting, prompt compression for long contexts, and common anti-patterns. This fills the gap between the three beginner prompting Concepts and the agent-building Field Guide chapters.
ideas.evidence: src/content/concepts/manifest.ts (prompting-basics, system-vs-user-prompts, few-shot-prompting all in Building Blocks group); src/content/deep-dives/en/ directory listing (no essay matching 'prompt-engineering', 'chain-of-thought-prompting', or 'advanced-prompting'); src/content/deep-dives/groups/architectures-and-patterns.ts (8 entries, none on prompt engineering); src/content/field-guide/en/f2.html (Field Guide prompts chapter assumes foundational knowledge but doesn't bridge to advanced techniques).
open_questions: Is Architectures & Patterns the right group for this essay, or should a new 'Prompting & Context' group be created alongside it?

Should chain-of-thought be covered here or left to the Reasoning & Test-Time Compute group which already has `chain-of-thought.html`? The distinction would be: this essay covers CoT as a prompting technique for practitioners; that group covers CoT as a compute mechanism.
ideas.mockup_hint: Header 'Deep Dive · Architectures & Patterns'. Step 1: why the prompt is the only interface an agent has with the model — the system prompt is the spec, and bad specs produce bad agents. Step 2: system prompt anatomy for agents — a labeled code block showing the six zones of a production agent system prompt (role, goal, capabilities, constraints, output format, examples). Step 3: chain-of-thought variants compared in a table (standard/zero-shot/least-to-most/structured), with one code block showing a structured CoT prompt. Step 4: anti-patterns — vague roles, contradictory constraints, missing output format, overlong examples. Close with a key-takeaway callout. zh: same structure, code blocks byte-identical, all prose translated.

ideas.title: Deep-Dive group header inconsistency: Safety group zh name mismatch
ideas.problem: The Safety & Security deep-dive group uses the en name 'Safety & Security' in the manifest (`safety-and-security.ts`) and 'Safety, Alignment & Agentic Security' in the actual HTML headers (observed in `agentic-threat-model.html`). The zh headers read '安全、对齐与智能体安全'. But the manifest `name` field in `safety-and-security.ts` has `L('Safety & Security', '安全与防护')`. This creates a mismatch: the index page groups entries under '安全与防护' (from the manifest) while the detail pages show '深入解析 · 安全、对齐与智能体安全' (from the HTML). The same mismatch exists in English: manifest says 'Safety & Security', detail pages say 'Safety, Alignment & Agentic Security'.
ideas.proposal: Align the group name across manifest and HTML headers. Either (A) update the manifest `safety-and-security.ts` name field to `L('Safety, Alignment & Agentic Security', '安全、对齐与智能体安全')` to match the more descriptive HTML headers; or (B) update all 9 safety deep-dive HTML files to use 'Deep Dive · Safety & Security' / '深入解析 · 安全与防护'. Option A is preferred — the longer name is more informative and the HTML files are the canonical authored content. This affects the index grouping label only, not any slug or route.
ideas.evidence:
src/content/deep-dives/groups/safety-and-security.ts line 5: `name: L('Safety & Security', '安全与防护')`; grep output of zh week headers shows `
深入解析 · 安全、对齐与智能体安全
` across 9 zh files; grep output of en week headers shows `Deep Dive · Safety, Alignment & Agentic Security` across 9 en files.
open_questions: Does '安全与防护' vs '安全、对齐与智能体安全' represent a meaningful conceptual difference that was intentional — e.g., the shorter name was chosen to keep the index column compact?
ideas.mockup_hint: No visual change needed — this is a data fix. After updating safety-and-security.ts name field, the index page groups under the longer descriptive label, matching what readers see when they open any individual essay in the group. No HTML file edits required for Option A.

notes: Overall content quality is high: zh translations are genuinely fluent (not machine-literal), the step/callout/qa structure is consistent across all 33 concepts and 75 deep-dives, and the Deep Dive header line convention (en/zh) is correctly applied to all 75 files. The two structural gaps that matter most for the 2026 landscape are: (1) the Retrieval & RAG deep-dive group is severely underthinned at 2 entries vs. the 5-9 norm — this is the highest-traffic topic area; (2) the multi-agent concept is entirely absent from the Concepts encyclopedia despite being heavily covered in Deep-Dives and Field Guide. The Safety group name mismatch (content-07) is a low-effort data fix that should be bundled with any PR touching that group. The key-takeaways gap (content-03) requires a coordinated authoring sprint across all 75 deep-dives — it is the highest-effort item and should be deprioritized relative to the net-new content gaps.
